title: Governor of Florida

context.text: Open seat: Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis is barred by the Florida Constitution from seeking a third consecutive term.
Republican primary (Aug. 18, 2026): U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds won with 47.8% of the vote, ahead of Lt. Gov. Jay Collins (25.2%), James Fishback (10.5%) and former House Speaker Paul Renner (8.5%).
Democratic primary (Aug. 18, 2026): former U.S. Rep. David Jolly won with 61.0%, ahead of Dayna Marie Foster (15.1%) and state Rep. Dotie Joseph (9.6%).
Florida candidates run as a ticket with a lieutenant governor running mate, who is chosen by the nominee and elected jointly with the governor candidate.

candidates.name: Byron Donalds
candidates.ballotNote: Running with Lt. Gov. candidate Bryan Avila, a former state senator. Won the Aug. 18 Republican primary with 47.8%.

summary.text: Byron Donalds is the Republican nominee for governor, running with former state Sen. Bryan Avila. He is the U.S. representative for Florida's 19th District (since 2021) and served in the Florida House from 2016 to 2020. His campaign platform emphasizes homeowners-insurance costs, healthcare price transparency, early-literacy and apprenticeship programs, requiring E-Verify, and cooperation with federal deportation efforts.

background.text: Born and raised in Crown Heights, Brooklyn; earned a B.A. in finance and marketing from Florida State University in 2002 and worked in finance, insurance and banking before entering politics.
Served in the Florida House of Representatives (District 80), 2016–2020, then was elected to the U.S. House in 2020 and re-elected in 2022 and 2024.

priorities.text: Lower insurance costs: protect recent insurance reforms and curb lawsuit abuse, keep Citizens Insurance small, and publish a consumer scorecard comparing insurers.
Healthcare price transparency: require providers to post cash prices for the 50 most common tests and procedures and guarantee cash patients the lowest rate offered to large insurers.
Education: train teachers in phonics-based reading instruction, provide state-funded tutoring for struggling third graders, and create apprenticeship pathways under 'LaunchPad Florida.'

positions.summary: Campaign plan calls for requiring E-Verify, cutting state funds that encourage illegal immigration, and coordinating state and local police with federal authorities to deport noncitizens who commit crimes.
positions.quote: Coordinate state and local police directly with federal authorities to quickly deport noncitizens who commit crimes in our communities.

positions.summary: Campaign education plan includes letting education money follow the student so parents can choose a school.
positions.quote: Let education money follow the student so parents can choose the best school for their child.

positions.summary: Voted yes on H.R. 28, the Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act, which passed the House 218–206.

record.text: Voted yes on H.R. 28, the Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act, which passed the House 218–206 with 1 voting present.
Voted yes on S. 5, the Laken Riley Act, which passed the House 263–156.
Voted yes on H.R. 1 (One Big Beautiful Bill Act), the motion to concur in the Senate amendment, which passed 218–214.
Sponsored H.R. 8371, the Reform Immigration Through Biometrics Act; referred to the House Subcommittee on Border Security and Enforcement.
Sponsored H.R. 9017, the Restore Florida Water Independence Act of 2026; referred to the House Subcommittee on Water, Wildlife and Fisheries.

candidates.name: David Jolly
candidates.ballotNote: Running with Lt. Gov. candidate Gwen Graham, a former U.S. representative. Won the Aug. 18 Democratic primary with 61.0%.

summary.text: David Jolly is the Democratic nominee for governor, running with former U.S. Rep. Gwen Graham. He represented Florida's 13th District as a Republican from 2014 to 2017, left the party in 2018, and joined the Democratic Party in 2025. His platform includes a state catastrophic-risk fund for property insurance, Medicaid expansion, a moratorium on hyperscale data centers, campaign-finance and ethics reform, and codifying the Roe/Casey abortion framework in Florida law.

background.text: Earned a B.A. from Emory University and a J.D. from George Mason University.
Served in the U.S. House for Florida's 13th District, 2014–2017, as a Republican; later an independent (2018–2022), a member of the Forward Party (2022–2025), and a Democrat since 2025.

priorities.text: Affordability and insurance: a state catastrophic fund to remove natural-disaster risk from the private insurance market and a state-backed loan program for condominium repairs.
Health care: expand Medicaid in Florida.
priorities.quote: Florida should commit to expanding Medicaid and ensuring healthcare for all Floridians.

priorities.text: A day-one moratorium on hyperscale data centers until environmental and water impacts are studied.
Campaign finance and ethics reform, and easier access to the ballot for citizen-initiated constitutional amendments.

positions.summary: Says Florida should codify the Roe/Casey framework if Congress does not restore it federally.
positions.quote: Absent federal legislation restoring these protections, Florida should codify the Roe/Casey framework.

positions.summary: Calls for banning assault-weapon sales, universal background checks, exploring licensing, and preserving and expanding red flag laws.
positions.quote: Florida should ban the sale of assault weapons, require universal and comprehensive background checks, explore licensing, and preserve and expand the red flag laws enacted following the tragedy at Parkland.

positions.summary: Calls for Florida to expand Medicaid.
positions.quote: Florida should commit to expanding Medicaid and ensuring healthcare for all Floridians.

positions.summary: Says Florida should accept climate science, invest in resiliency, and require greater integration of clean energy in public utilities.
positions.quote: Florida should accept the science of climate change, protect our beaches and state parks, and invest in resiliency throughout the state.

positions.summary: Calls for increased funding for public schools and for holding voucher schools to public-school standards, and says the voucher program should be means-tested rather than eliminated.
positions.quote: The voucher program should be means-tested to ensure funding is provided for families with demonstrated economic need.

record.text: Voted yes on H.R. 596, the bill to repeal the Affordable Care Act, which passed the House 239–186.
Voted yes on the motion to concur in the Senate amendment to H.R. 3762, the fiscal-year 2016 budget reconciliation bill; it passed 240–181.
Sponsored H.R. 4443, the Stop Act, which would bar federal officeholders from personally soliciting campaign contributions; he gave introductory remarks on the floor and no further action followed.

researchNotes: Running mates (Bryan Avila with Donalds; Gwen Graham with Jolly; and the others noted in each summary) are elected jointly and are not listed as separate entries. The slate matches the Florida Division of Elections candidate listing for the Nov. 3, 2026 general election (Donalds, Jolly, Jewett, Burkett, Russo, Dimanche, Abrams, Datto), which also lists write-in candidates Kathy Anderson and Erik Morris; write-ins are not included here. Primary percentages come from the Wikipedia race page; the state's results site could not be loaded. Ballotpedia was blocked by a bot challenge from this environment. Federal roll-call votes were checked against the House Clerk's published records and bill sponsorships against Congress.gov bill-status data; Donalds's Florida House record (2016–2020) was not researched. The independent candidates have no research beyond the ticket listing.
